scenes.heading: Design a YouTube Analytics Pipeline
scenes.subheading: Views, watch time, and trends at scale
scenes.narration: Let us design a pipeline that ingests billions of video events per day and turns them into creator dashboards and trending analytics with both real-time and historical views.

scenes.heading: Requirements to nail first
bullets: Ingest massive view and watch-time events
Real-time counts plus accurate daily rollups
Deduplicate replays and filter bot traffic
Serve creator dashboards with low latency
scenes.narration: First we pin down requirements. We must ingest an enormous, spiky stream of view, watch-time, and interaction events. We need near real-time counters for live dashboards alongside accurate daily aggregates for reporting. We have to deduplicate repeated events and filter out bot and fraudulent traffic so metrics are trustworthy. And we must serve creator dashboards with low latency across many concurrent users.

scenes.heading: End-to-end architecture
steps: Raw events land in the lake (Bronze)
Batch builds Silver and Gold rollups
scenes.narration: Clients emit events into a partitioned Kafka log that absorbs the spiky, high-volume traffic. A stream-processing job consumes that log to maintain live, approximate counters for the real-time dashboard. In parallel, raw events are persisted to the lake as an immutable Bronze layer. Scheduled batch jobs then clean, deduplicate, and aggregate that data into Silver and Gold rollups by video, creator, and day. A fast serving store exposes the results to dashboards.

scenes.heading: Real-time counts vs batch rollups
scenes.narration: The real-time layer delivers counts within seconds, which is essential for live view counters, but it is approximate and may temporarily double-count before deduplication. The batch layer runs hours behind but produces deduplicated, bot-filtered, authoritative numbers suitable for reporting and creator payouts. Serving both from one place gives creators a lively live number that later reconciles to the trusted daily figure, which is a classic reason to blend streaming and batch.

scenes.heading: Deduplication and bot filtering
bullets: Assign each play a unique event id
Dedupe on id within a time window
Detect bots by rate and behavior signals
Count a view only past a watch threshold
scenes.narration: Trustworthy metrics hinge on cleaning the stream. Each play event carries a unique event id so retries and replays can be deduplicated within a time window. Bot and fraudulent traffic is detected using rate limits and behavioral signals, then excluded. A view is only counted once watch time crosses a defined threshold, so accidental clicks do not inflate numbers. These rules live in the batch layer where completeness allows accurate judgments, which is why batch numbers are the ones used for payouts.

scenes.heading: Scaling and cost choices
bullets: Partition the log by video id for parallelism
Store raw events in cheap object storage
Tier old raw data to cold storage
scenes.narration: At this scale, cost and throughput drive design. Partitioning the event log by video id lets processing parallelize massively across consumers. Raw events are kept in cheap object storage as the replayable source of truth. Frequently queried rollups, such as views by video and day, are pre-aggregated so dashboards read small, fast tables rather than scanning raw events. And older raw data is tiered to colder, cheaper storage, since it is rarely reprocessed but must remain available for audits and backfills.

scenes.text: Use a replayable log, a real-time counter layer, and accurate batch rollups so dashboards feel live yet reconcile to trusted numbers.
scenes.narration: The winning design pairs a replayable event log with a fast approximate counter layer and accurate deduplicated batch rollups, so dashboards feel live in the moment yet always reconcile to numbers you can bill and report on.
